PIT-Wasserstein metrics for miscalibration diagnosis

Source: vignettes/pit-w-metrics.Rmd

We simulated sets of forecasts with known location bias and predictive spread to examine how the three PIT-Wasserstein scores distinguish these sources of miscalibration, and compared the scores with the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and interval coverage. The simulations provide the results in Figure 1 of the paper.

1. The simulation

We compare the scores across a range of ratios of reported spread to error spread, \(\sigma_\mathcal{S}/\sigma_\mathcal{E}\). A ratio below one represents overconfidence and a ratio above one represents underconfidence.

1.1 The error-function model

Each simulated estimator is defined by two distributions, following the structure introduced in vignette("introduction-to-pit"):

Component Symbol Role
error distribution \(\mathcal{E} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\mathcal{E}, \sigma_\mathcal{E})\) Difference between the central estimate and the reference value
spread distribution \(\mathcal{S} \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\sigma_\mathcal{S}, \kappa_\mathcal{S})\) Uncertainty reported for each prediction

For each of the estimator’s predictions \(i\) we draw a true value \(x_i\), an error \(e_i \sim \mathcal{E}\) and a claimed uncertainty \(s_i \sim \mathcal{S}\), and emit the probabilistic prediction

\[ \hat{X}_i \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_i + e_i,\; s_i\right) \]

The simulations vary three aspects of the forecasts.

  • \(\mu_\mathcal{E}\) — bias. The systematic displacement of the central estimate. Zero means unbiased.
  • \(\sigma_\mathcal{S}/\sigma_\mathcal{E}\) gives the spread ratio, labelled calibration in the code and used on the horizontal axes.
  • \(\kappa_\mathcal{S}\) is the coefficient of variation of the reported uncertainty, labelled “CI variation” in the figures. At zero, every prediction reports the same spread. At larger values, reported spread varies independently of the errors, a form of miscalibration we call spread–error decoupling.

The spread distribution is lognormal (lnorm4, parametrised by median and coefficient of variation) because a claimed uncertainty must be positive and because it makes \(\kappa_\mathcal{S}\) scale-free.

1.2 The parameter sweep

We simulate 1,000 estimators, each making 1,000 predictions. We draw the bias, error scale, typical reported spread and variation in reported spread once per estimator, and a reference value, a location error and a reported spread for each prediction.

Parameter Drawn as Range
true values \(x_i\) \(\mathrm{Uniform}(-1, 1)\) per prediction
bias \(\mu_\mathcal{E}\) \(\mathrm{Uniform}(-1, 1)\) per estimator
error scale \(\sigma_\mathcal{E}\) \(\log\)-uniform \([\tfrac12, 2]\)
claimed scale \(\sigma_\mathcal{S}\) \(\log\)-uniform \([\tfrac12, 2]\)
decoupling \(\kappa_\mathcal{S}\) \(\mathrm{Uniform}(0, 2)\) per estimator

The independent log-uniform draws of \(\sigma_\mathcal{S}\) and \(\sigma_\mathcal{E}\) give ratios from \(\tfrac14\) to 4. The log scale places a ratio of \(\tfrac12\) the same distance from one as a ratio of 2. We draw bias independently of the ratio so that we can compare scores at similar ratios for estimators with different biases.

bias_limit = 1
conf_range = 2

config = tibble(
  sd_sd_mean = c(conf_range),
  sd_label = forcats::as_factor(c("heterogenous CIs"))
) %>%
  group_by(sd_label, sd_sd_mean) %>%
  reframe(
    samples = 1000,
    bias_dist = "norm",
    bias_location = runif(1000, -bias_limit, bias_limit),
    bias_scale = exp(runif(1000, -log(conf_range), log(conf_range))),
    sharpness_dist = "lnorm4",
    sharpness_location = exp(runif(1000, -log(conf_range), log(conf_range))),
    sharpness_scale = runif(1000, 0, sd_sd_mean)
  )

generate_simulation() expands that configuration into 1000 × 1000 individual predictions, and prediction_scores() collapses each estimator’s 1000 predictions back to one row of scores.

sim = config %>% generate_simulation(true_value_fn = function(n) runif(n, -1, 1))
#> interfacer: development mode active (test environment).
#> This message is displayed once every 8 hours.
#> Warning: unexpected groups in the return value of generate_simulation(...):
#> observed: sd_label+sd_sd_mean+samples+bias_dist+bias_location+bias_scale+sharpness_dist+sharpness_location+sharpness_scale+link+dist+run_id+calibration+adjust
#> expected: <any>+dist+link+calibration+adjust
#> Warning: ireturn validation did not pass without changing the value.
scores = sim %>% prediction_scores()

2. The metrics

Full definitions and derivations are in the paper; this is the working summary. For each estimator, the PIT values \(u_i = F_i(x_i)\) are sorted and compared against the uniform plotting positions \(r_i = (i - \tfrac12)/n\):

\[ B_{pit} = \frac1n\sum_i \left| r_i - u_{(i)} \right| \]

This is the 1-Wasserstein distance to a discrete uniform distribution on the \(n\) midpoints. The distance to the continuous uniform distribution differs by at most \(1/(4n)\). Even independent uniform PIT values generally give a positive score in a finite sample.

The bias adjustment estimates one location shift, \(\hat\delta = \mathrm{median}_i(g(m_i) - g(x_i))\) on the link scale, applies it to the observations, and recomputes the PIT values as \(u^{adj}\). Applying the same two summaries to the adjusted values gives

\[ U_{pit} = \frac1n\sum_i \left| r_i - u^{adj}_{(i)} \right|, \qquad D_{pit} = \frac1n\sum_i \left( r_i - u^{adj}_{(i)} \right)\mathrm{sgn}\!\left(\tfrac12 - r_i\right) \]

\(U_{pit}\) measures the remaining distance after fitting the common shift. For a forecast with intervals that are too narrow, the low PIT values fall below their ranks and the high PIT values exceed theirs. The signed weight makes both contributions positive. Intervals that are too wide tend to give negative contributions in both halves. Departures in opposing directions can cancel in \(D_{pit}\).

Metric Range Reads
\(B_{pit}\) \([0, \tfrac12]\) total miscalibration, bias included
\(U_{pit}\) \([0, \tfrac12]\) miscalibration with bias removed
\(D_{pit}\) \([-\tfrac14, \tfrac14]\) signed dispersion error: \(+\) over-confident, \(-\) conservative

All three are returned by prediction_scores() alongside the mean CRPS and coverage probabilities.

3. Figure 1

Each panel plots one score for all 1,000 estimators against the spread ratio \(\sigma_\mathcal{S}/\sigma_\mathcal{E}\) on a log scale. The vertical line marks a ratio of one, where the typical reported spread matches the spread of the errors.

# estimator SD/error SD:
# ratio between the SD of an estimate and the SD of the error function
# a low value means that the estimate is more confident than it should be
# a high value says it is too conservative

# Panel A: mean CRPS

p2a = ggplot(
  scores,
  aes(x = calibration, y = mean_crps, colour = abs(bias))
) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Absolute bias",option = "magma") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = Inf,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = Inf,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  ylab("Mean CRPS") +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  xlab("estimator SD/error SD")

# Panel B: baseline PIT-Wasserstein

## Combined 4 panel plot

plot_metrics = patchwork::wrap_plots(
  p2a,
  p2b,
  p3a,
  p3b,
  ncol = 2,
  guides = "collect",
  axes = "collect"
) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

.gg_save_as(
  plot_metrics,
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig1-metric-compare"),
  size = std_size$two_third,
  formats = c("pdf", "eps")
)

Mean CRPS (panel A) was lowest near a spread ratio of one among estimators with little bias. At similar spread ratios, the larger values generally came from estimators with greater absolute bias. The baseline PIT-Wasserstein score \(B_{pit}\) also increased with bias and away from a spread ratio of one (panel B).

The adjusted score \(U_{pit}\) was lowest near a spread ratio of one (panel C). At similar ratios, \(U_{pit}\) tended to be higher when reported uncertainty varied more independently of error, as measured by \(\kappa_\mathcal{S}\).

The directed score \(D_{pit}\) crossed zero near a spread ratio of one (panel D). Negative values indicate conservative forecasts and positive values indicate overconfident forecasts. The crossing was similar across values of \(\kappa_\mathcal{S}\), and the curve was approximately symmetric about it on the log scale.

\(D_{pit}\) indicates the direction of the spread discrepancy. \(U_{pit}\) also responds to departures that cancel in the signed score. The significance vignette describes how to compare their values with reference distributions.

3.5 Comparison with interval coverage

We also calculated how often the reference value fell inside the reported intervals.


ggplot(
  scores,
  aes(x = calibration, y = mean_coverage.0.5, colour=sharpness_scale)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  ylab("50% coverage probability") +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "CI variation") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  xlab("estimator SD/error SD")

Coverage increased with the spread ratio and changed little at the extremes shown here. Each coverage estimate describes one interval level. The PIT-Wasserstein scores use information from across the predictive distribution.
